lesson.title: The Full Picture: Slice Notation with Step
lesson.summary: The complete slice syntax start:stop:step adds a third number that controls how many indices to skip between characters, enabling tricks like taking every other character or reversing a string outright.
lesson.body:
Basic slicing with word[start:stop] always walks forward through a string one character at a time. The full slice syntax adds a third piece, word[start:stop:step], where step controls the size and direction of each jump between characters. When step is left out, Python defaults it to 1, which is exactly the ordinary forward slicing already covered. Setting step to 2 collects every second character, setting it to 3 collects every third, and a negative step reverses the direction of travel entirely, walking backward through the string instead of forward.

Take "PYTHON" once more and apply a step of 2 across the whole string:

word = "PYTHON"
print(word[::2])

Leaving start and stop both empty means the slice spans the entire string, from index 0 through the end, and a step of 2 means only every other index is collected: 0, 2, and 4. Those indices hold P, T, and O, so the result is "PTO". Indices 1, 3, and 5, holding Y, H, and N, are skipped entirely because the step jumps over them.

A step of -1 produces one of the most useful one-liners in Python, reversing a string outright:

print(word[::-1])

With start and stop both left empty and step set to -1, Python starts at the last character and walks backward to the first, collecting N, O, H, T, Y, and P in that order, producing "NOHTYP". This works because a negative step flips the default direction of start and stop as well: when step is negative and no explicit start or stop is given, Python begins at the end of the string and moves toward the beginning, rather than beginning at index 0 as it does for a positive step.

All three parts of a slice can be combined at once. word[1:6:2] starts at index 1, stops before index 6, and takes every second character in between: index 1 is Y, index 3 is H, index 5 is N, so the result is "YHN". Index 2 and index 4 are skipped over because the step is 2 rather than 1. Working out a slice like this by hand, listing out the exact indices the step will land on before checking which characters sit there, is the most reliable way to avoid off-by-one mistakes until the pattern becomes second nature.

This full three-part slice syntax is not unique to strings; it works identically on lists and other sequence types in Python, which is one of the reasons it is worth mastering carefully here. Once you are comfortable reading start:stop:step on a string like "PYTHON", that same mental model, walk from start toward stop, jumping step indices at a time, transfers directly to slicing any other sequence you encounter later.

A step can never be 0; writing word[::0] raises a ValueError, because a step of 0 would mean never moving to a new index at all, and Python refuses to even attempt a slice that could never finish. It is also worth noticing that a negative step combined with an explicit start and stop still obeys the half-open rule from ordinary slicing, just walking in the opposite direction: word[5:1:-1] starts at index 5, moves backward, and stops before reaching index 1, collecting indices 5, 4, 3, and 2, which on "PYTHON" spells out "NOHT". Working through a few of these by listing the exact indices visited, in order, before looking up each character, is the fastest way to build confidence with step values before relying on them in real code.
